'''Raymond C. Stevens''' (born 1963) is an American [[chemist]] and [[Structural biology|structural biologist]],  Founder, CEO and Board Member of Structure Therapeutics;<ref name="structuretx.com">https://structuretx.com/</ref> Founding Director of the {{Proper name|iHuman Institute}} at [[ShanghaiTech University]]; Professor Emeritus of Chemistry, and Founding Director of the Bridge Institute at the [[University of Southern California]]; Board Member, Danaher Corporation.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://investors.danaher.com/2017-02-21-Danaher-Announces-Appointment-of-Raymond-C-Stevens-Ph-D-to-Danaher-Board|title = Danaher Announces Appointment of Raymond C. Stevens, Ph.D. To Danaher Board}}</ref>

==Biography==
Stevens was born into a military family. In 1969 his father died in the [[United States Air Force|Air Force]], and his mother took several part-time jobs to support the family. He was raised in [[Auburn, Maine]].

In 1980, Stevens joined the Army under their split option training program and conducted basic training at [[Fort Dix]], [[New Jersey]] and advanced individual training at [[Fort Sam Houston]], [[Texas]]. While engaged in his military service, Stevens entered the [[University of Southern Maine]] in the Computer Science program in 1981. However, an enthusiastic professor (John Ricci) converted him to the study of [[Chemistry]]. He spent two summers working as an intern at the [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]] in [[Long Island]] with Professor Ricci, and Drs. Thomas Koetzle and Dick McMullan, where he first learned how to determine the molecular structure of compounds by [[X-ray diffraction|X-ray]] and [[neutron diffraction]]. While there he also met a [[University of Southern California]] research team led by Dr. Robert Bau; after he obtained a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in chemistry at USM, he entered the [[University of Southern California]] in pursuit of a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree in Chemistry working with Professor Robert Bau and Nobel Laureate Professor, [[George Olah]]. He completed his Ph.D. in 26 months, graduating in 1988.<ref name="Emerson">{{cite news |last1=Emerson |first1=Eva |title=Fast-Tracking Lifesaving Discoveries |url=http://college.usc.edu/news/stories/410/fast-tracking-lifesaving-discoveries/ |accessdate=2 August 2018 |work=USC Dornsife |date=1 October 2007}}</ref>

Although science is a major part of his life, Stevens climbs mountains with his wife and children and runs [[ultramarathon]]s including the [[Vermont 100 Mile Endurance Run]]<ref>[http://www.vermont100.com/html/2006_results.html/ Vermont100 race results 2006]</ref> and [[American River 50 Mile Endurance Run]],<ref>[http://ultrasignup.com/results_participant.aspx?fname=Raymond&lname=Stevens&age=0/ American River 50 Miler race results]</ref> and in 2011 he successfully completed the 156 mile [[Marathon des Sables]]<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.darbaroud.com/index_uk.php# |title= 26th SULTAN MARATHON DES SABLES|website=www.darbaroud.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903030419/http://www.darbaroud.com/index_uk.php |archive-date=2011-09-03}}</ref> across the Moroccan Sahara Desert. Currently working on climbing the 7 highest mountains on the 7 continents, he has climbed Mt. Kilimanjaro, Mt. Elbrus, Aconcagua, Vinson Massif and Mt. Kosciuszko.  Next mountains are Mt. Everest and Denali.

==Scientific career==
After obtaining his Ph.D., Stevens accepted a postdoctoral position in 1988 in the lab of Nobel Laureate [[William Lipscomb|William N. Lipscomb, Jr.]] in the chemistry department at [[Harvard University]] where he focused on the large allosteric [[enzyme]] [[aspartate carbamoyltransferase]].<ref>
Stevens, R. C., & Lipscomb, W. N., "Allosteric Enzymes" Eds., R. Diamond, T. F. Koetzle, K. Prout, & J. Richardson, ''Molecular Structures in Biology'' (Oxford, UK: Oxford University Press, 1993) pp. 223–259.
</ref><ref>
Stebbins, J. W., Robertson, D. E., Roberts, M. F., Stevens, R. C., Lipscomb, W. N., & Kantrowitz, E. R., "Arginine 54 in the active site of Escherichia coli aspartate transcarbamoylase is critical for catalysis: A site-specific mutagenesis, NMR, and X-ray crystallographic study," Prot. Sci. 1, 1435–1446 (1992).
</ref><ref>
Stevens, R. C., & Lipscomb, W. N., "A molecular mechanism for pyrimidine and purine nucleotide control of aspartate transcarbamylase," Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 89, 5281–5285 (1992).
</ref><ref>
Stevens, R. C., Reinisch, K. M., & Lipscomb, W. N., "Molecular Structure of Bacillus subtilis Aspartate transcarbamoylase at 3.0 A Resolution," Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 88, 6087–6091 (1991).
</ref><ref>
Stevens, R. C., Chook, Y. M., Cho, C. Y., Lipscomb, W. N., & Kantrowitz, E. R., "Escherichia coli aspartate carbamoyltransferase: The probing of crystal structure analysis via site-specific mutagenesis," Protein Engineering 4, 391–408 (1991).
</ref><ref>
Gouaux, J. E., Stevens, R. C., & Lipscomb, W. N., "Crystal Structures of Aspartate Carbamoyltransferase Li gated with Phosphonoacetamide, Malonate and CTP or ATP at 2.8-A Resolution and Neutral pH," Biochemistry 29, 7702–7715 (1990).
</ref><ref>
Stevens, R. C., J.E. Gouaux, & Lipscomb, W. N., "Structural Consequences of Effector Binding to the T State of Aspartate Carbamoyltransferase Crystal Structures of the Unligated and ATP- and CTP-Complexed Enzymes at 2.6-A Resolution," Biochemistry 29, 7691–7701 (1990).
</ref><ref>
Stevens, R. C., & Lipscomb, W. N., "Allosteric control of quaternary states in E. coli aspartate transcarbamylase," Biochemistry and Biophysics Research Communications 171, 1312–1318 (1990).
</ref><ref>
Gouaux, J. E., Stevens, R. C., Ke, H., & Lipscomb, W. N., "Crystal structure of the Glu-239 to Gln mutant of aspartate carbamoyltransferase at 3.1 A resolution: An intermediate quaternary structure," Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. USA 86, 8212–8216 (1989).
</ref>
In 1991, he accepted a [[tenure-track]] position at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in the chemistry department with a joint appointment in neurobiology. His initial research as an assistant professor focused on structural neurobiology and immunology, combining chemistry, structural biology and protein chemistry with a specific biological interest in understanding how the [[G protein-coupled receptor]] (GPCR) superfamily works. A seminal collaboration for Stevens was with Professor [[Peter G. Schultz]] where they jointly published a series of ''Science'' and ''Nature'' papers describing the immunological evolution of antibodies through careful structural studies.<ref>H. D. Ulrich, E. Mundorff, B. D. Santarsiero, E. M. Driggers, R. C. Stevens and P. G. Schultz (1997) The interplay between binding energy and catalysis in the evolution of a catalytic antibody Nature 389: 271–5</ref><ref>G. J. Wedemayer, P. A. Patten, L. H. Wang, P. G. Schultz and R. C. Stevens (1997) Structural insights into the evolution of an antibody combining site Science 276: 1665–9</ref><ref>F. E. Romesberg, B. Spiller, P. G. Schultz and R. C. Stevens (1998) Immunological origins of binding and catalysis in a Diels-Alderase antibody Science 279: 1929–33</ref><ref>A. Simeonov, M. Matsushita, E. A. Juban, E. H. Thompson, T. Z. Hoffman, A. E. t. Beuscher, M. J. Taylor, P. Wirsching, W. Rettig, J. K. McCusker, R. C. Stevens, D. P. Millar, P. G. Schultz, R. A. Lerner and K. D. Janda (2000) Blue-fluorescent antibodies Science 290: 307–13</ref> In 1999, Stevens left Berkeley to take a [[tenured]] position at [[The Scripps Research Institute]]. While at The Scripps Research Institute, Stevens has helped to found and establish the Joint Center for Structural Genomics,<ref>[http://www.jcsg.org/ www.jcsg.org]</ref> Joint Center for Innovative Membrane Protein Technologies,<ref>[http://jcimpt.scripps.edu/ jcimpt.scripps.edu]</ref> and the GPCR Network,<ref>[http://cmpd.scripps.edu/ cmpd.scripps.edu]</ref> all funded by the [[National Institutes of Health]] with direct guidance from [[NIGMS]].  In 2012, Stevens co-founded the {{Proper name|iHuman Institute}} at [[ShanghaiTech University]].<ref>ihuman.shanghaitech.edu.cn</ref> In 2014, Stevens moved his lab from The Scripps Research Institute to the [[University of Southern California]], where he is currently the Provost Professor of Biological Sciences and Chemistry and he founded the Bridge Institute to converge the arts and sciences.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.utsandiego.com/news/2014/jun/23/tamiflu-USC/|title = The San Diego Union-Tribune - San Diego, California & National News}}</ref>

Stevens is known for obtaining the structures of many biologically significant proteins and his technological innovations. He is considered a pioneer of [[high-throughput screening|high-throughput]] [[x-ray crystallography]] and structural genomics.<ref>R. C. Stevens and I. A. Wilson  (2001)  Tech.Sight. Industrializing structural biology. Science 293: 519-20</ref> His laboratory has led to the contribution of over 500 [[protein structure]] entries in the [[Protein Data Bank]] www.pdb.org. Stevens has withdrawn two different structures of ligand-bound clostridial neurotoxins.<ref>M. A. Hanson, R. C. Stevens (2009) Retraction: Cocrystal structure of synaptobrevin-II bound to botulinum neurotoxin type B at 2.0 A resolution Nat Struct Mol Biol. 16(7):795.</ref><ref>M. A. Hanson, T. K. Oost, C. Sukonpan, D. H. Rich, R. C. Stevens (2002) Structural Basis for BABIM Inhibition of Botulinum Neurotoxin Type B Protease [J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2000, 122, 11268−11269] J. Am. Chem. Soc. 124(34):10248–10248</ref>

In October 2007, Stevens and colleagues published the first high-resolution structure of a human [[GPCR]].<ref>[http://www.usc.edu/schools/college/news/october_2007/stevens.html USC College : News : October 2007 : Raymond Stevens]</ref><ref>V. Cherezov, D. M. Rosenbaum, M. A. Hanson, S. G. Rasmussen, F. S. Thian, T. S. Kobilka, H. J. Choi, P. Kuhn, W. I. Weis, B. K. Kobilka and R. C. Stevens (2007) High-resolution crystal structure of an engineered human beta2-adrenergic G protein-coupled receptor Science 318: 1258–65.</ref>  The β<sub>2</sub>-[[adrenergic receptor]] work was quickly followed up 9 months later by the determination of the structure of the human A<sub>2A</sub> [[adenosine A2A receptor|adenosine receptor]] structure,<ref>V. P. Jaakola, M. T. Griffith, M. A. Hanson, V. Cherezov, E. Y. Chien, J. R. Lane, A. P. Ijzerman and R. C. Stevens (2008) The 2.6 Angstrom Crystal Structure of a Human A2A Adenosine Receptor Bound to an Antagonist, Science 322: 1211–7</ref> also known as the [[caffeine]] receptor. In 2010, the structures of the human [[chemokine]] [[CXCR4]] receptor (HIV co-receptor),<ref>B. Wu, E.Y.T. Chien, C.D. Mol, G. Fenalti, W. Liu, V. Katritch, R. Abagyan, A. Brooun, P. Wells, F.C. ==Structure based drug discovery==
In 1992, Stevens worked with researchers at [[Gilead Sciences|Gilead]] on the structural studies of [[neuraminidase inhibitor]]s that eventually became [[Tamiflu]],<ref>C. U. Kim, W. Lew, M. A. Williams, H. Liu, L. Zhang, S. Swaminathan, N. Bischofberger, M. S. Chen, D. B. Mendel, C. Y. Tai, W. G. Laver and R. C. Stevens (1997) Influenza neuraminidase inhibitors possessing a novel hydrophobic interaction in the enzyme active site: design, synthesis, and structural analysis of carbocyclic sialic acid analogues with potent anti-influenza activity J Am Chem Soc 119: 681–90;</ref><ref>M. A. Williams, W. Lew, D. B. Mendel, C. Y. Tai, P. A. Escarpe, W. G. Laver, R. C. Stevens and C. U. Kim (1997) Structure-activity relationships of carbocyclic influenza neuraminidase inhibitors Bioorg Med Chem Lett 7: 1837–1842;</ref><ref>C. U. Kim, W. Lew, M. A. Williams, H. Wu, L. Zhang, X. Chen, P. A. Escarpe, D. B. Mendel, W. G. Laver and R. C. Stevens (1998) Structure-activity relationship studies of novel carbocyclic influenza neuraminidase inhibitors J Med Chem 41: 2451–60.</ref> and later partnered with Roche. After the initial experience with structure based [[drug discovery]] from 1992 to 1997 with [[Gilead]] and [[Tamiflu]], Stevens focused on understanding the basic mechanism of how Botox ([[botulinum toxin]]) works, and on ways to use this scaffold for next generation protein therapeutics. In parallel to the work on [[botulinum toxin]], he worked on the enzymes involved in the [[catecholamine]] biosynthetic pathway, specifically the three aromatic amino acid hydroxylases including [[phenylalanine hydroxylase]]. From 1999 to 2004, Stevens was involved in the startup of Syrrx that developed the marketed drug Nesina for type II diabetes. From 2000 to 2010, Stevens has worked with [[BioMarin Pharmaceutical]] to develop Kuvan ([[tetrahydrobiopterin]]) and assisted in the design and development of PEG-PAL (pegylated [[Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase]]) as treatments for mild and classical [[phenylketonuria]] (PKU).<ref>H. Erlandsen and R. C. Stevens (1999) The structural basis of phenylketonuria Mol Genet Metab 68: 103–25</ref><ref>L. Wang, A. Gamez, H. Archer, E. E. Abola, C. N. Sarkissian, P. Fitzpatrick, D. Wendt, Y. Zhang, M. Vellard, J. Bliesath, S. M. Bell, J. F. Lemontt, C. R. Scriver and R. C. Stevens (2008) Structural and biochemical characterization of the therapeutic Anabaena variabilis phenylalanine ammonia lyase J Mol Biol 380: 623–35.</ref><ref>T. S. Kang, L. Wang, C. N. Sarkissian, A. Gamez, C. R. Scriver and R. C. Stevens (2010) Converting an injectable protein therapeutic into an oral form: Phenylalanine ammonia lyase for phenylketonuria, Mol Genet Metab 99: 4–9.</ref>  In 2008, Stevens started Receptos that developed an S1P1 agonist for multiple sclerosis and inflammatory bowel disease, now on the market called Zeposia and sold by BMS.<ref name="nationalmssociety.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.nationalmssociety.org/About-the-Society/News/FDA-Approves-Oral-Zeposia%C2%AE-(Ozanimod)-for-Relapsin#:~:text=The%20U.S.%20Food%20and%20Drug,is%20now%20available%20for%20prescription |title=UPDATE: FDA-Approved Oral Zeposia® (Ozanimod) for Relapsing Forms of MS Now Available for Prescripti &#124; National Multiple Sclerosis Society |publisher=Nationalmssociety.org |date= |accessdate=2022-06-21}}</ref>

==Biotechnology Startups==
Stevens has started four biotechnology companies (Syrrx (1999), MemRx (2002), Receptos (2009), and RuiYi (2011)), all focused on structure based drug discovery and each company started with one of his former Ph.D. students.

*Syrrx, started with UC-Berkeley Ph.D. student [[Nathaniel David]] and colleague [[Peter G. Schultz]], was acquired by [[Takeda Pharmaceuticals]] in 2005 for the high-throughput structure based drug discovery platform, and because of a phase II clinical candidate [[alogliptin]] known to inhibit the enzyme [[DPPIV]] and is now an approved drug known as Nesina.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Somers|first1=Terri|title=Japanese drug giant taking over Syrrx here|url=http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/uniontrib/20050208/news_1b8syrrx.html|accessdate=9 August 2016|publisher=San Diego Union-Tribune|date=8 February 2005}}</ref> 
*MemRx, started with Ph.D. student Mike Hanson and Jun Yoon, was acquired by Sagres Discovery in 2003 for the membrane protein expression technologies, and the combined entity was later acquired by [[Novartis]] in 2005. 
*Receptos,<ref>[http://www.receptos.com/ www.receptos.com]</ref> started with Ph.D. students Mike Hanson, Chris Roth and staff scientist Mark Griffith along with TSRI colleagues Hugh Rosen and Ed Roberts, focused on GPCR structure based drug discovery with a primary interest in [[inflammation]] and [[oncology]]. On July 14, 2015, [[Celgene]] announced that it will buy Receptos for $7.32 billion in cash.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/money/business/2015/07/14/celgene-receptos/30168919/|title = $7.3B deal: Celgene will buy drug firm Receptos|website = [[USA Today]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2015/07/14/celgene-to-acquire-receptos-for-more-than-7b.html|title=Celgene to acquire Receptos for $7.2 billion|website=[[CNBC]]|date=14 July 2015}}</ref> The S1P1 agonist was approved for patients with MS in March, 2020 under the brand name Zeposia and sold by BMS.<ref name="nationalmssociety.org"/>
*In 2011, Stevens, with Paul Grayson and his former TSRI graduate student Fei Xu, started RuiYi, a biologics GPCR company located in Shanghai, China. The company was acquired by Anaphore in 2012.<ref>[http://www.ruiyibio.com www.ruiyibio.com]</ref>  The company currently has one drug in phase II clinical trials for RA and a drug in place for liver fibrosis.
*In 2018, Stevens, with former students Mike Hanson and Jun Yoon, started Structure Therapeutics,<ref name="structuretx.com"/> a company focused on converting biologics to small molecules using next generation structure-based drug discovery to make best in class medicines accessible to all. The company currently has two drugs in clinical trials for pulmonary and metabolic diseases.<ref>{{cite press release | url=https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220801005172/en/Structure-Therapeutics-Extends-Financing-Advances-Diabetes-and-Obesity-Clinical-Program-and-Changes-Name-from-ShouTi | title=Structure Therapeutics Extends Financing, Advances Diabetes and Obesity Clinical Program and Changes Name from ShouTi | date=August 2022 }}</ref>

==Philanthropy==

=== The John S. Ricci Lecture Hall ===
Stevens honored his University of Southern Maine professor and mentor, John Ricci, by facilitating the renovation of the lecture hall inside the University science building and renaming it The John S. Ricci Lecture Hall.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://usm.maine.edu/publicaffairs/world-renowned-scientist-and-usm-alumnus-recognizes-professor-mentor | title=World-renowned scientist and USM alumnus recognizes professor & mentor &#124; Office of Public Affairs &#124; University of Southern Maine }}</ref>

=== The Professor Emeritus John Ricci Undergraduate Fellowships ===
Established by Stevens to honor USM Professor Emeritus John Ricci and his innovative educational program at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]], these summer fellowships offer a unique opportunity for USM undergraduates to pursue research at [[The University of Southern California]] in Los Angeles, California, one of the oldest private research universities.<ref>[http://stevens.scripps.edu/Ricci.html/ TSRI Stevens Lab: John Ricci Undergraduate Fellowship ]</ref> In 2018, Stevens and his wife supported the building of the John S. Ricci Lecture Hall in honor of his undergraduate teacher and mentor.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.pressherald.com/2018/04/01/bill-nemitz-maine-professor-struggling-student-had-a-chemistry/|title=Bill Nemitz: Maine professor, struggling student had a chemistry|newspaper=Press Herald |date=April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://usm.maine.edu/publicaffairs/world-renowned-scientist-and-usm-alumnus-recognizes-professor-mentor|title = World-renowned scientist and USM alumnus recognizes professor & mentor &#124; Office of Public Affairs &#124; University of Southern Maine}}</ref>

=== The Robert Bau Endowed Graduate Fellowship ===
Established by Stevens and Charles McKenna in 2010 to honor [[University of Southern California|USC]] distinguished professor Robert Bau after his death in December 2008, the fellowship proposes to help celebrate Professor Bau's life and honor his extraordinary mentorship by linking him to new generations of young chemists at USC.<ref>[http://chem.usc.edu/dept/bau.html/ USC Department of Chemistry: In Memoriaum-Robert Bau]</ref>
